Chapter 1

Architecture

1.1  Repository layout (monorepo)1.2  Runtime topology1.3  Laravel module structure (modular monolith)1.4  Architecture Decision Records

1.1Repository layout (monorepo)

webapp/                      (JMN monorepo root)
├── apps/
│   ├── api/                 Laravel 13 API: authoritative business logic (PHP 8.4)
│   ├── web/                 Next.js 16 / React / TypeScript: public site, newsroom, admin UI
│   └── mobile/              Flutter: audience + reporter apps (flavours)
├── infra/
│   ├── yegara/              cPanel deployment: cron, .htaccess, deploy scripts
│   ├── scaled/              supervisor / nginx / systemd templates for VPS/K8s migration
│   └── ci/                  CI helper scripts
├── docs/                    This documentation set (source of truth for engineering)
└── .github/workflows/       CI pipelines

1.2Runtime topology

Browser / App ──► Cloudflare (DNS, CDN, WAF, TLS, bot, rate limit)
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
     Next.js (SSR/ISR)     Laravel API  /api/v1  (+ /install, /health)
          │  server-side fetch  │
          └──────────►──────────┘
                     │
        PostgreSQL 16+ (authoritative)   Redis (cache, queues, locks, rate limits)
                     │
        Storage driver (local | S3-compatible | R2)  ──► CDN
                     │
        Queue workers: critical, high, default, media, ai, analytics, low
                     │
        MediaProcessor driver (local-ffmpeg | provider)
The Next.js server never holds business rules. It calls the Laravel API with the user's session token (an httpOnly cookie that only the Next.js server reads). The browser never sees API tokens for staff sessions.

1.3Laravel module structure (modular monolith)

app/
├── Domain/<Module>/            Models, Enums, Events, Policies, Services (actions), Rules, Exceptions
├── Http/Controllers/Api/V1/<Module>/   Thin controllers: validate, authorize, call a service, return a resource
├── Http/Requests/<Module>/     FormRequest validation
├── Http/Resources/<Module>/    JSON:API-style resources
├── Http/Middleware/            RequestId, SecurityHeaders, InstallGuard, ForceJson, SetLocale
├── Infrastructure/             Drivers: AI, Media, Search, Social, Storage, Webhooks
├── Jobs/                       Queue jobs (one queue per priority)
└── Support/                    ApiResponse, Ulid helpers, Money, Blocks
Module rules 1. A module may use another module only through its public Services, Events or Contracts. It must never write another module's tables directly. 2. Cross-module side effects run through domain events plus listeners (queued where they are expensive).

  1. Each module owns its migrations, prefixed by module: 2026_10_01_000100_identity_....
  2. Controllers contain no business logic.

Modules: Identity, Organization, Security (RBAC and audit), Language, Editorial (content), Workflow, Assignment (newsroom), FactCheck, Investigation, Media, Video, Audio, Podcast, Live, Archive/Search, Knowledge, Audience, Comments, Newsletter, Social, Advertising, Analytics, AI, Notifications, Webhooks, Administration (settings, flags, health), Installer.

1.4Architecture Decision Records

ADR-001: Modular monolith

Accepted. It deploys simply on cPanel and supports shared transactions. Boundaries are enforced by convention plus an architecture test (Pest arch()): Domain code must not depend on the Http layer.

ADR-002: ULID primary keys

Accepted. Every domain table uses a char(26) ULID primary key (HasUlids). ULIDs are time-sortable, so they index better than UUIDv4. Public URLs use ULIDs plus slugs. Reference tables (languages, countries) use natural codes as unique keys and keep ULID PKs for consistency.

ADR-003: Translations as rows

Accepted. The articles table stores language-neutral data. article_translations has a unique key on (article_id, language_id). UI strings live in ui_translations.

ADR-004: Block-based body stored as JSONB

Accepted. article_translations.body is JSONB, {version:1, blocks:[{id,type,data}]}, validated server-side against the registry in App\Support\Blocks\BlockRegistry. HTML is never stored as the source of truth. A plain-text projection feeds search.

ADR-005: Immutable versions + audit log

Accepted. article_versions rows are insert-only (a DB trigger rejects UPDATE and DELETE). audit_logs is insert-only and hash-chained (prev_hash, hash = sha256), so tampering is detectable.

ADR-006: Optimistic concurrency

Accepted. lock_version integer on articles, translations and assignments. Clients send If-Match: <lock_version> or a lock_version field; a mismatch returns 409 EDIT_CONFLICT with the current server version. There is no silent overwrite.

ADR-007: Queue profiles

Accepted. QUEUE_CONNECTION=redis, falling back to database. Queues: critical, high, default, media, ai, analytics, low.

  • yegara profile: a cron job runs php artisan schedule:run every minute, and the scheduler runs queue:work --stop-when-empty --max-time=50 per queue group.
  • scaled profile: supervisor or Horizon runs workers per queue.

ADR-008: Next.js deployment

Accepted. output: 'standalone'. On Yegara it runs through cPanel "Setup Node.js App" (Passenger) where available; otherwise it runs on a separate Node host. ISR and tag revalidation are triggered by Laravel webhooks to /api/revalidate (HMAC-signed).

ADR-009: Provider drivers

Accepted. These contracts live in App\Infrastructure\*\Contracts: AiProvider, MediaProcessor, LiveProvider, SearchEngine, SocialPublisher, PushSender. Drivers are selected in config by environment variables.

ADR-010: Degraded mode without Redis

Accepted. If Redis is unavailable, cache, queue and session fall back to database. The Health Center reports "degraded".

ADR-011: Multilingual search

Accepted. search_documents table: a tsvector column built with languages.search_config, plus a pg_trgm GIN index on the normalised text. Queries combine websearch_to_tsquery with trigram similarity for non-stemmed scripts.

ADR-012: Staff vs audience identities

Accepted. The users table is for staff (Sanctum guard staff). audience_users is for readers (Sanctum tokens on a separate abilities namespace). Staff permissions can never be granted to audience accounts.

ADR-013: API response envelope

Accepted. Success: {success:true, data, meta?, links?, request_id}. Error: {success:false, error:{code,message,details}, request_id} (spec §125).

2.3Cross-cutting middleware (order)

  1. RequestId: assign/propagate X-Request-Id, and add it to the Log::withContext and the queue job payload.

  2. SecurityHeaders

  3. ForceJsonResponse (api group)

  4. SetLocale (from ?lang / Accept-Language, validated against active languages)

  5. EnsureInstalled (returns 503 NOT_INSTALLED until installed, except for /install and /health)

  6. Throttle by the named limiters of doc 13 §5

  7. auth:sanctum plus EnsureMfa for sensitive groups

2.4Exception rendering

bootstrap/app.php → withExceptions: map ValidationException → 422 VALIDATION_FAILED, AuthenticationException → 401, AuthorizationException → 403 FORBIDDEN, ModelNotFound → 404 <MODEL>_NOT_FOUND, ThrottleRequests → 429, ApiException → its code and status, anything else → 500 SERVER_ERROR (logged with the request_id; message hidden).

2.5Services contract style

Services are final classes with constructor injection. Public methods take explicit typed arguments or DTO arrays that have already been validated, and wrap their mutations in DB::transaction(). Events are dispatched with afterCommit (ShouldDispatchAfterCommit).

2.6Jobs & queues

Jobs declare $queue from App\Support\Queues constants (CRITICAL, HIGH, DEFAULT, MEDIA, AI, ANALYTICS, LOW), have $tries, a backoff() method, and a failed() method that records the failure. The request_id is propagated through a job middleware.

2.7Console commands

jmn:publish-scheduled, jmn:expire-content, jmn:audit:verify, jmn:search:reindex, jmn:health, jmn:queue:cron-work (the cPanel profile), jmn:install (CLI installer), jmn:backup (pg_dump plus a media manifest).

2.8Testing

The test DB is PostgreSQL (jmn_test), never SQLite, because the triggers, JSONB and tsvector must be real. The RefreshDatabase trait with seeders LanguageSeeder and RbacSeeder. The factories cover all models.

3.3Data access

  • src/lib/api.ts is a server-only fetch wrapper. It reads JMN_API_URL and forwards the X-Request-Id and the staff token taken from the httpOnly jmn_staff cookie, and it returns typed results or throws ApiError.
  • Public pages use fetch(..., { next: { revalidate: 60, tags: ['article:ID', 'home:LANG'] } }).
  • /api/revalidate (a route handler) verifies the HMAC from Laravel and calls revalidateTag.
  • Staff mutations use Server Actions, which call Laravel. The browser never receives the bearer token.

3.4Design system (§52, §164, §165)

Tokens are CSS variables: colours (--jmn-ink, --jmn-paper, --jmn-accent #B3122E, --jmn-breaking), spacing on a 4px scale, and type scales for Latin, Ethiopic and Arabic stacks. The components are Button, Badge (breaking/live/opinion), Card, Headline, Byline, Block renderers and LanguageSwitcher. Everything uses logical properties so it is RTL-safe.

3.5Accessibility (§85)

There is a skip link, landmarks, a visible focus ring, colour contrast ≥ 4.5:1, lang/dir on the html element and on mixed-language fragments, alt text required at media upload (enforced in the API for publication), captions for video, and support for prefers-reduced-motion. Playwright + axe runs on the home, article and login pages in CI and must report zero serious or critical violations.

3.6Performance (§86)

The targets are LCP < 2.5s on 3G-fast, JS < 120KB gz on article pages (mostly RSC), next/image with width-based variants from the API, and fonts subset with display=swap.

3.7PWA (§54, §55)

There is a manifest.webmanifest and a service worker that caches the app shell plus up to 50 saved articles (stale-while-revalidate), with an offline fallback page.

3.8Public website redesign (implemented, sprint 7)

Design system (src/app/globals.css, src/app/fonts.css) - Tokens as CSS variables with light/dark themes (html[data-theme], auto follows the OS). The toggle stores the choice in localStorage only, so pages stay statically cacheable (no cookie). An inline bootstrap script sets it before first paint. - Self-hosted variable fonts in public/fonts (OFL): Inter (UI), Source Serif 4 (headlines and reading), Noto Sans/Serif Ethiopic (am, ti, …), Noto Naskh Arabic. unicode-range means each reader downloads only the scripts on the page. There are no third-party font requests, and builds need no network. - Script-aware typography: data-font switches body and headline families. Arabic is never letter-spaced or upper-cased, because that breaks glyph joining. Logical properties are used throughout for RTL. - Components: ui/StoryCard (lead, feature, standard, compact, text, overlay, opinion variants), ui/Media (Img with srcset from API variants, fixed aspect ratio so there is no layout shift, lazy loading, high-priority lead image), chrome/Interactive (theme toggle, drawer, reading progress, share bar, view beacon), LiveBlog (20 s polling; new entries wait behind an "n new updates" button).

Pages - Masthead: date line, edition bar, menu drawer (search, all sections, all editions), sticky section nav and a breaking ticker (scrolls only with 3+ alerts). - Front page: editor-built modules rendered as a newspaper front. The band holds latest, the lead with a second tier, and most read. Section blocks alternate treatments; there is an opinion band and a dark fact-check band with verdict colours. With no editor layout, the default layout is hero, most read, latest, fact checks, more. - Article: breadcrumb, type badges, serif display headline, byline (links to the author page), dates, reading time (Intl plurals), share bar (native share, WhatsApp, Telegram, X, Facebook, copy link), hero image with caption and credit, corrections, fact-check box, body with drop cap, pull quotes, fact boxes and images, live blog, "also available in" edition cards, newsletter call-to-action, sticky most-read rail, related stories. - Structured data: NewsArticle, Opinion or Analysis article, or LiveBlogPosting; BreadcrumbList; ClaimReview; the NewsMediaOrganization site-wide; hreflang alternates; OG/Twitter large images. - Section fronts (lead, top four, most read, paginated archive with rel=prev/next), author profile pages (ProfilePage JSON-LD), search, newsletter landing (no data collected until the Audience module), styled 404 inside the edition shell.

Same-origin routes - /media/{id}/w{320|640|1024|1600}.webp proxies API public variants. - /api/view is the aggregate view beacon. It fires after 4 s and respects Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control. - /api/live/{id} is live-blog polling.

3.9Newsroom application shell & UI kit (implemented, sprint 16)

Shell (components/newsroom/NewsroomShell.tsx, nav model lib/newsroom-nav.ts) - Desktop ≥1024 px: fixed dark sidebar grouped Newsroom · Publishing · Audience & revenue · Administration, Lucide-style inline SVG icons (Icon.tsx, no icon font), active item with accent bar; collapsible to a 72 px icon rail, remembered in the jmn_nav cookie so the server renders the final state (no flash). - Phones/tablets: sticky top bar (hamburger, brand, page title, search, New story, account menu). The hamburger opens an off-canvas drawer: focus-trapped, inert when closed, Esc/backdrop/navigation close it, page scroll locked, slides from the logical start edge (correct in RTL). - Phones: bottom tab bar (four most relevant desks for this person + a raised New story button + More → drawer), safe-area aware. - Command palette (CommandPalette.tsx): ⌘K / Ctrl+K or / anywhere; n = new story. Jump to any permitted desk, create, or search headlines; full keyboard support and ARIA combobox/listbox semantics. - Account menu: roles, MFA state, view site, sign out. Route-level loading.tsx skeleton, error.tsx boundary (with digest reference), branded not-found.tsx. - Navigation is filtered by permission (any-of), editorial and commercial desks stay separate; the API still authorises every call.

UI kit (components/newsroom/ui.tsx, server-safe): PageHeader (eyebrow, back link, actions), Card, Stat, Badge (7 tones), StatusPill (workflow states), Notice, EmptyState, Tabs (bookmarkable, scroll-fade on phones, 44 px targets), Toolbar + SearchField/SelectField, DataTable (stacks into labelled cards under 768 px via data-label), Split (main + side rail), Pager, ButtonLink, fmtRelative, humanize.

CSS layer (globals.css, @layer components): .nr-card, .nr-input, .nr-label, .nr-table(-stack), .nr-fade-x; legacy desk controls inside .nr-shell main inherit the same input/select/file/checkbox styling so every desk is consistent.

Rebuilt screens: login (split brand panel), dashboard (greeting, alarm notice, KPI stats, review queue, latest activity, scheduled, deadlines, desk-at-a-glance), stories (status tabs, search, responsive table), story editor (edition tabs with live dots, counters, word count / read time, inline workflow with contextual inputs, timeline history, versions), new story (type picker, edition, priority), and every desk: fact checks, investigations, comments, page builder (module cards with reorder/remove), live, podcasts (+ episode workspace with publishing panel), newsletters, social, analytics, advertising, and the administration console.

QA gate: Playwright at 1440×900 and 390×844 across 29 routes and 4 roles: HTTP 200, scrollWidth equals the viewport (no horizontal overflow), zero console errors; palette, rail persistence, drawer and 404 are exercised.

3.10Story Studio

components/newsroom/studio/* is the only editor of article bodies. It is lossless: every block type in BlockRegistry (26 types) loads, edits and saves with all fields intact. A feature test round-trips each type.

Files: - schema.ts: block definitions, normalise, serialise, problems, word count. - Fields.tsx: auto-growing text, inline marks, media and story pickers, grid fields. - StoryStudio.tsx: canvas, inserter and slash menu, toolbar, tabs (Write / Preview / SEO & social). - VersionHistory.tsx: word-level diff and restore.

Interaction: - / opens the slash menu. - Enter adds a paragraph. - ⌘↑/⌘↓ moves a block; drag handles also move blocks. - ⌘D duplicates a block; delete is undoable. - ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z undo and redo, coalesced to 1 s. - ⌘S saves.

Inline marks: - Syntax: **bold**, *italic*, [text](https://…). - They are stored as plain text and parsed by Blocks.tsx Inline into React nodes. No HTML is ever stored or injected. - Links must be https.

Drafts: unsaved work is kept in localStorage (jmn:studio:{article}:{lang}). A recovery banner offers restore or discard. Server saves use lock_version; a stale save receives 409 EDIT_CONFLICT and nothing is overwritten.

Preview: desktop, tablet and mobile widths, rendered with the public Blocks component, plus Google, Facebook and X previews that use the social title and description.

Page mode: the same editor edits /newsroom/pages/[kind].

Secondary bar (sticky) Home · every section · divider · Fact Check (accent colour) · Live video (dot when on air) · Podcasts all widths; scrolls sideways on small screens

Breaking-news alerts sit directly below the masthead.

Mobile: menu · logo · LIVE badge (only when something is on air) · search · compact edition code (e.g. EN) · account. The theme toggle moves into the drawer.

Edition selector (EditionMenu): - It replaces the old separate language strip and is built as a disclosure menu. - Each edition shows its native name and its English name. - The current edition is highlighted. - Keyboard: Enter or Space opens it with focus on the current edition. ↑ and ↓ move through the list. Home and End jump to the first and last edition. Esc closes it and returns focus to the button; Tab also closes it. Clicking outside closes it. - Each link sets lang, dir and hreflang. - Without JavaScript, the drawer and the footer still list every edition.

Footer (SiteFooter, four bands): 1. Newsletter title, text and Sign up, beside Follow MediaOS: up to 9 edition social icons (44 px targets, https only, rel="noopener noreferrer me", each labelled "… (opens in a new tab)").

  1. Logo, mission and quick links (Live, Podcasts, Digital newspaper, Topics, Notifications, RSS), then four groups: All sections, Our journalism, About MediaOS, Legal and policies (with Cookie settings when consent is enabled).

  2. Editions as pills in their own script, lang/dir/hreflang on each, the current one highlighted.

  3. © line, Privacy, Terms, Accessibility and bureaus. - Phones: each group is a <details> disclosure. From 768 px up, FooterGroupsSync keeps them open, so assistive technology sees open columns as well, not just the CSS. - Pages come from the edition. An edition without its own page links the default edition's page with an EN badge and hreflang. - Policy pages render note blocks with the edition's labels (note.editors_note, note.correction, note.update, note.source).

Verified: no horizontal overflow and no off-screen controls at 1440, 1100, 768, 390 and 360 px. The header was also checked in /ar (RTL) and /am (Ethiopic).

3.12Staff Center and public staff pages (October 2026)

Newsroom - /newsroom/staff (staff.manage): Toolbar filters plus a DataTable. - /newsroom/staff/{id|me}: StaffProfileForm, with per-edition <details> carrying lang/dir, working-language chips, up to 10 https links, a "Staff desk only" fieldset for managers, and a lock_version conflict message. - /newsroom/admin/users/{id}/offboard: open-work summary plus OffboardForm. - /newsroom/admin/integrations: state badges (Working, Set up, Needs attention, Not set up, No official integration), each with the next action.

Public - /{lang}/staff: search, department and working-language filters, featured first, CollectionPage/ItemList JSON-LD; filtered views are noindex,follow. - /{lang}/author/{slug} adds beat, coverage, expertise, languages (native names with lang), rel="me" links, Person sameAs/knowsLanguage/knowsAbout, og:type=profile with the photo or brand card, and hreflang only for editions with their own wording. - The footer About MediaOS group links the directory. - ShareBar adds LinkedIn (share-offsite) and mailto:. - Article metadata always has an image (the brand 1200×630 card as fallback), og:site_name, article:author (profile URLs) and article:tag.

3.13Email Center (October 2026, directive §11–16)

Newsroom (email.manage or email.approve; translators see only their editions) - /newsroom/email - Matrix of the 21 system emails × editions. Each cell is Approved, Pending, Draft, Uses English or Off, and its accessible name is a full sentence. - Filters by category, language and search. - Pending-approval list. - Warning when the mailer is log. - Approvers also get Delivery log. - /newsroom/email/{key}/{code} (EmailTemplateEditor) - Edition switcher. - Fields: subject, preheader, heading, body, CTA label and small print, each with the edition's lang/dir. - Variable insert buttons; only catalogued {{variables}} are accepted. - Save draft / Submit for approval. - Approve/Reject panel for a different approver; a rejection needs a note. - More actions: discard draft, restore default, copy from another edition or version, switch on/off. Required security mail cannot be switched off. - Preview in a sandbox="" iframe, the plain-text version, Send me a test (own address, [TEST] subject), and version history. - /newsroom/email/log - Recent deliveries with masked address, status and rendered language. No bodies. - /newsroom/staff/me - Email preferences (tasks, queries, mentions, returned, published, assignments, alerts). Security mail is always sent.

Login - /newsroom/login links Forgot your password?. - /newsroom/login/forgot: always check your inbox. - /newsroom/login/reset?token=: new password plus confirmation, with the password rules shown.

Chapter 4

Database design

4.1  Conventions4.2  Reference data4.3  Identity4.4  Organization4.5  RBAC & security4.6  Taxonomy4.7  Editorial4.8  Workflow4.9  Assignments4.10  Fact-check & investigations4.11  Media4.12  Search & knowledge4.13  Platform4.14  Seeds (§193–195)

4.1Conventions

  • PostgreSQL ≥ 16 (dev runs 17). Extensions: pg_trgm, unaccent, citext.
  • PK id char(26) ULID. FKs are <entity>_id char(26), with ON DELETE RESTRICT unless noted.
  • created_at/updated_at timestamptz. Soft delete (deleted_at) only where marked SD.
  • Enumerations are varchar + CHECK constraints (they are easier to migrate than PG enums). Allowed values are listed here and mirrored in PHP backed enums.
  • JSONB for structured flexible data (blocks, settings, metadata), with GIN indexes where queried.
  • Every multi-tenant table carries organization_id.
  • Insert-only tables are protected by the trigger jmn_forbid_mutation() (IO).
  • All times are stored in UTC and rendered in the user or bureau timezone (§110).

Chapter 5

Security internals

5.1  Threat model (summary)5.2  Authentication5.3  Authorization5.4  Permission catalogue (initial)5.5  HTTP security5.6  Audit (§84)5.7  Privacy (§107, §108)5.8  Investigations and confidential sources (implemented)

5.1Threat model (summary)

Asset Threats Controls
Staff accounts Credential stuffing, phishing, session theft Rate limits, lockout, TOTP MFA, device list, token revocation, suspicious-login events
Published journalism Unauthorised publish/alter, insider tampering Server-side policies, workflow permissions, immutable versions, hash-chained audit
Confidential sources / investigations Data leak, insider access Encrypted columns, membership ACL, is_sensitive permissions, access audit
Media uploads Malware, polyglot files, SSRF, path traversal MIME sniffing (finfo), allow-list, size caps, randomised names, private disk, image re-encode
API Injection, IDOR, mass assignment Eloquent parameter binding, FormRequests, policies on every record, $fillable allow-lists, ULIDs
Audience PII Breach, over-collection Minimisation, separate guard, export/delete (DSR), retention jobs
Installer Takeover after install Lock file + DB flag; /install returns 404 once installed

5.2Authentication

  • Passwords use bcrypt (cost 12) or argon2id when available. The minimum is 12 characters, checked against the Laravel Password::defaults() rules plus an uncompromised check (optional; requires outbound access).
  • Lockout: after 5 failures in 15 minutes, locked_until = now + 15 min and the account returns ACCOUNT_LOCKED. The lockout is recorded as a security_events entry of severity medium. Each attempt is recorded in login_attempts.
  • A suspicious login is one from a new IP/UA pair for the user, or from a new country if the Cloudflare CF-IPCountry header is present. It produces a suspicious_login event and a notification.
  • MFA uses TOTP (RFC 6238, via google2fa). The secret is stored encrypted, and there are 10 one-time recovery codes, stored hashed. MFA is mandatory for roles flagged requires_mfa (executive_admin, system_admin, security_admin, editor_in_chief, managing_editor). Such users receive only a limited-ability token until MFA is enrolled. The web enrolment flow at /newsroom/mfa works as follows:
  • The login stores the enrolment token in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie scoped to /newsroom/mfa that lasts 15 minutes.
  • The QR code is rendered server-side as SVG with bacon-qr-code, so the secret never reaches a third-party QR service.
  • Recovery codes are shown once.
  • Staff single sign-on (task T19) with Google Workspace and Microsoft Entra ID is off until configured: JMN_STAFF_SSO_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID/_SECRET, or JMN_STAFF_SSO_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID/_SECRET/_TENANT_ID (a tenant GUID; common/organizations are refused). Register the redirect URI {JMN_SITE_URL}/newsroom/login/sso/google or /microsoft with the provider.
  • Authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), a single-use state bound to the provider (10 minutes) and a single-use nonce. The ID token is verified locally: RS256 against the provider's JWKS, issuer, audience, expiry.
  • Only existing, active staff accounts sign in; nobody is created. JMN_STAFF_SSO_DOMAINS (comma-separated) limits the accepted address domains.
    • Google requires email_verified and a Workspace account (hd, within the domains when they are set). A consumer Google account on a company address is refused.
    • Microsoft requires the configured tenant (tid).
  • On its first single sign-on, a staff account is bound to the provider's stable ID (Google sub, Microsoft oid; table staff_sso_identities; audited as auth.sso_linked). From then on that ID signs in, not the address, so a different identity that merely carries the same address is refused (docs/41 S41-M4).
  • The state is also bound to the browser that started the sign-in: an httpOnly cookie holds its digest for 10 minutes, so a callback link started elsewhere is refused (login CSRF, S41-L5). Refusals are recorded as sso_failed security events.
  • SSO replaces only the password step. Lockout, the is_active check, the TOTP challenge and mandatory MFA enrolment apply unchanged. Sign-ins are audited as auth.login with method: sso_google|sso_microsoft; refusals are recorded in login_attempts. The routes have their own limit (20 per minute per IP).
  • On the web, a pending authenticator challenge waits in an HttpOnly cookie scoped to /newsroom/login for 5 minutes, never in the URL.
  • SAML 2.0 (2.2.0; JMN_STAFF_SSO_SAML_*, off until the IdP entity ID, https SSO URL and an RSA ≥ 2048 signing certificate are set): SP-initiated only. The AuthnRequest (HTTP-Redirect, unsigned) is single-use behind a random RelayState (10 minutes); the ACS (/api/v1/auth/saml/acs) accepts a Response only if it is ≤ 256 KB, has no DOCTYPE (parsed with LIBXML_NONET), holds exactly one Assertion directly under the Response, every ds:Signature sits on the Response or that Assertion with Reference = the parent's ID and that ID unique in the document (signature wrapping), transforms enveloped + exc-c14n only, SHA-256/512 digest, RSA-SHA256/512 verified against the configured certificate (KeyInfo ignored); then Destination and Recipient = ACS, Issuer = IdP, Audience = SP entity ID, Status Success, time window with 3-minute skew, InResponseTo = our request, assertion ID not replayed (cache until expiry). Encrypted assertions and transient NameIDs are refused. The ACS issues a 2-minute one-time code bound to the RelayState (and so to the browser's state cookie); the newsroom exchanges it like an OIDC code. Accounts bind to the NameID (provider = saml).
  • Passkeys (WebAuthn, task T19) for staff and readers are off until JMN_PASSKEYS=true. They use web-auth/webauthn-lib (MIT).
  • The relying party is the host of JMN_SITE_URL. JMN_PASSKEY_RP_ID can name a parent domain instead, and JMN_PASSKEY_ORIGINS adds further web origins (e.g. the jmn.et alias).
  • User verification (fingerprint, face or device PIN) is required. Attestation is "none", so no device data is collected. The origin is pinned, the signature counter must move forward (a cloned authenticator is refused), and each sign-in challenge is single-use (5 minutes).
  • Sign-in is discoverable: the browser offers the account. The user handle is a keyed hash, never an e-mail address or an ID. A reader's passkey is never a staff sign-in.
  • Staff: a passkey is added or removed only from a session that passed the authenticator code, when the account has one. By owner decision (4 Nov) a user-verified passkey counts as both factors (JMN_STAFF_PASSKEY_SATISFIES_MFA=true, the default). Set it to false to have an enrolled authenticator still ask for its code.
  • Either way the TOTP authenticator remains the fallback, roles that require MFA must still enrol it, and lockout and the active check apply. Sign-ins are audited as auth.login with method: passkey. Adding and removing a passkey is audited (auth.passkey_added / auth.passkey_removed). A known credential that fails verification is recorded in login_attempts as passkey_failed.
  • Readers manage passkeys under account Settings. Passkeys are listed in the data export (name and dates) and deleted on erasure.
  • Sessions and devices (task T19): staff (My profile) and readers (account Settings) see every live session: device name, browser, created and last used, with the current one marked. They can sign out one session or every other one.
  • A staff session also shows its address. Staff sign-outs are audited (auth.session_revoked, auth.sessions_revoked).
  • A reader session keeps only the browser string, never the address. It is included in the export and deleted on erasure.
  • The web passes the visitor's address (X-Forwarded-For, trusted only from TRUSTED_PROXIES) and browser on every staff and reader sign-in call. Lockout per source and new-device alerts therefore see the person, not the web server.
  • Tokens: Sanctum personal access tokens with abilities staff, mfa, with expiry (default 12h staff, 30 days mobile with refresh). Logout revokes the token.

5.3Authorization

  • PermissionService::userCan(User, permissionKey, ?scopeContext). It resolves roles, including scoped roles (bureau, desk, language, section, country), and caches the resolved permission set in Redis per user (for 5 minutes). The cache is busted when roles change.
  • Laravel Gate::before for super_admin only (system_admin is not a bypass by default).
  • Policies per model: ArticlePolicy, AssignmentPolicy, MediaPolicy, UserPolicy, InvestigationPolicy.
  • Scope semantics: a role granted with scope desk:X applies only to resources whose desk_id = X. Language scope applies to translations in that language.

5.4Permission catalogue (initial)

article.create article.view_any article.edit_own article.edit_any article.submit article.review
article.approve article.schedule article.publish article.publish_breaking article.correct
article.unpublish article.archive article.restore article.delete
translation.edit translation.complete factcheck.work factcheck.complete
assignment.view assignment.create assignment.manage
media.upload media.view media.manage liveblog.post
newsroom.view_dashboard newsroom.view_all
investigation.view investigation.manage source.view_identity(sensitive)
user.view user.manage role.assign(sensitive) audit.view(sensitive)
settings.manage(sensitive) language.manage health.view
ads.manage analytics.view newsletter.manage social.manage ai.use ai.manage
The default role matrix is defined in database/seeders/RbacSeeder.php, which is the source of truth.

5.5HTTP security

  • Headers from the SecurityHeaders middleware: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, Permissions-Policy, and a CSP (API: default-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none').
  • The web app (next.config.ts) sends an allow-list CSP with default-src 'self', object-src 'none', base-uri 'self', form-action 'self' and frame-ancestors 'self'. Scripts come from self plus inline, for the Next bootstrap, JSON-LD and the theme script.
  • Nonces were rejected deliberately: they would force every page to render per request and defeat ISR caching on shared hosting.
  • The web app also sends X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Permissions-Policy and HSTS. /newsroom/* is no-store and noindex.
  • Staff session cookies are HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax.
  • CORS: an allow-list of origins from the JMN_CORS_ORIGINS env var.
  • trustProxies is configured for Cloudflare, with the real IP taken from CF-Connecting-IP.

5.6Audit (§84)

Audited: authentication events, role changes, every workflow transition, publish, unpublish, correct, settings changes, investigation/source access, exports and AI output acceptance. Each record is chained: hash = sha256(prev_hash || canonical_json(record)). php artisan jmn:audit:verify recomputes the chain and reports the first broken link.

5.7Privacy (§107, §108)

  • Audience PII is kept to a minimum: email, display name, preferences.
  • Data subject requests: an export (JSON) and a deletion (anonymise comments, delete account). Both are audited.
  • Analytics store IPs truncated (/24 for IPv4, /48 for IPv6), never the raw IP.
  • Retention: login_attempts are kept 180 days, security events 2 years, analytics raw events 13 months, then aggregated.

5.8Investigations and confidential sources (implemented)

  • Encrypted at rest with the application key (encrypted casts): investigation title/summary, dossier entries, source identity/contact/notes. Database dumps and backups contain ciphertext only; losing APP_KEY makes them unrecoverable — store it in the password manager with the backup password.
  • Audit entries never contain confidential values (field names and lengths only); reasons for reveals and purges are recorded.
  • source_access_logs and investigation_notes are immutable (DB trigger).
  • Membership e-mails carry only the codename.
  • API responses are Cache-Control: no-store, private; web pages are noindex and dynamic.
  • AI confidentiality gate: AiAssistant refuses every AI action on an article linked to an investigation that is not cleared for publication. It returns 403 AI_CONFIDENTIAL and audits ai.refused_confidential. The optional exception requires JMN_AI_PRIVATE_PROVIDER=true, a configured Ollama driver, and a loopback, localhost, RFC1918 IPv4, or IPv6 unique-local endpoint. A provider flag alone or a public hostname/IP does not qualify. Production operators must still verify network routing and endpoint ownership before enabling the exception.

Document ID: JMN-DOC-044 · Prepared: 6 November 2026 · Status: Governing plan for the phase after 1.2.0, for owner review

Question answered: How should MediaOS grow from a complete single-server newsroom platform into a media platform that any outlet can run, from a small newsroom on shared hosting to a global broadcaster, with every capability ready to switch on when the infrastructure exists?

This document is the plan. The detail for each area lives in the companion files in docs/next-phase/:

File Covers
A — Live production, contribution and broadcast see Product Bible Guests on WhatsApp, Telegram, Zoom, Meet, Teams, Jitsi, SIP and plain phones; multiple studios; radio and TV; restreaming everywhere at once; hardware; satellite, remote servers and streaming devices; file transfer
B — Audience interaction, contributors and moderation see Product Bible One interaction centre for comments, questions, polls, likes and views from every platform; non-staff op-eds and opinion; audience reporting; notifications and reminders
C — Digital asset management and archive see Product Bible Folders, collections, search, rights, retention, storage tiers and the full who/when/what record
D — Edge, speed, security, privacy and safe upgrades see Product Bible CDN, Cloudflare, image optimisation, bot and human verification, consent and terms, permissions, offline, SEO, zero-downtime upgrades
E — Built-in AI see Product Bible OCR, image optimisation, text to speech, speech to text, subtitles, fraud and intrusion detection, automated moderation
F — Typography and design language see Product Bible Font stack per script, licensing, type scale, broadcast graphics type
G — Provider interfaces (developer reference) see Product Bible The PHP contracts, registry, health checks and contract tests to build

Sources are listed at the end of each companion file. Facts that could not be confirmed are marked [verify].

6.1Summary for the owner

  1. The 1.2.0 platform is broad and well built, but it has never run in production. No server, no real studio PC, no real phone, no CI run on GitHub. The single most valuable next step is still the one in the existing backlog: deploy 1.2.0 for real (tasks T1–T3, T29–T31 in REMAINING-TASKS.md). Everything in this document assumes that happens first, and nothing here should delay it. You said the same: let the developers finish the simple version, then proceed.
  2. Your thesis is right where it matters most and wrong as a blanket rule. A media platform must not depend on one outside service for anything that can be taken away from it: guest contribution, live distribution, telephony, messaging, payments, storage, AI engines and the CDN. MediaOS already does this in places (social, payments, TTS, phone and live drivers), and the Broadcast model is engine-neutral. But putting every component behind a pluggable interface would cost a great deal and buy little. §3 says exactly where abstraction pays and where it does not.
  3. The key design idea is "normalise, don't integrate". MediaOS does not need a deep integration with WhatsApp, Zoom, Telegram, Meet and Teams separately. It needs one media hub that accepts a small set of open protocols (SRT, WHIP, RTMP, SIP, NDI on the studio LAN) and a set of recipes that turn any outside app into one of them. A WhatsApp call becomes a SIP or WebRTC audio leg; a Zoom guest becomes an NDI or SRT feed; a plain phone call becomes SIP. After that, every guest looks the same to the studio, the rundown, the recorder and the archive. This keeps the number of moving parts small while keeping every option on the table.
  4. A capability tier model (§4) makes "click a button to turn it on" honest. Five tiers, from shared hosting (Tier 0) to global (Tier 4). Each capability has providers per tier, a default, a fallback chain and a checklist of what infrastructure it needs. A new Capabilities page in administration shows every capability, what it would take to enable it, and a switch that turns on only when its requirements pass a health check. A switch cannot create a server, but once the server exists, enabling the feature is a setting, not a development project.
  5. Most of the switch machinery already exists and only needs to be unified: Docker compose profiles (vdo-ninja, owncast, clamav, transfer, onion, ai), per-edition Pennant flags, the encrypted settings store for keys, and provider registries in five domains. §5 describes the one Capability Registry that joins them.
  6. Seven new things are worth building, in this order (§7): the Capability Registry; a professional DAM and archive layer; a unified Interaction Centre; a Guest Gateway with Jitsi or LiveKit plus a SIP bridge for phones and WhatsApp; a self-hosted multistream fan-out; a contributor (op-ed) desk; and an AI moderation and OCR layer, which also replaces the dependence on Google's Perspective API (it shuts down after 31 December 2026).
  7. Product scope is decided (6 November 2026): MediaOS is its own platform, installable by other outlets. Each outlet runs its own single-tenant copy and switches capabilities on for its tier. A multi-tenant hosted service stays possible later but is not designed in now. The remaining decisions that need you are in §8.

6.2Honest assessment of the platform today

2.1 What is strong

Area Evidence
Editorial core 16 editions, block editor with immutable versions (ADR-004/005), 13-state workflow, four-eyes publishing with MFA, fact-check and investigation workspaces, corrections log
Broadcast core Channels, programmes, EPG, rundowns, prompter, HTML graphics, as-run log, studio devices and command queue, stream destinations, contribution sessions, MOS 2.8.5 gateway and CasparCG playout in Studio Bridge (doc 26 §4)
Engine neutrality already started StudioEngine (OBS, Meld) with engine-neutral obs.* commands; StreamPlatform lists 15 destinations including custom SRT and WHIP
Pluggable drivers already started SocialDriverRegistry (10 platforms), GatewayRegistry (Chapa, ArifPay, manual…), LiveProviderRegistry (manual, Mux), TtsEngine (Kokoro, Piper, HTTP), PhoneGateway (Africa's Talking, log), SearchEngine, MediaProcessor, MalwareScanner, ContentCredentialsTool
Resilience Onion service, mirrors, signed endpoint list with app failover, shutdown mode, Lite edition, emergency static snapshot, stale-if-error (doc 36)
Self-hosted AI with licence discipline services/ai-worker refuses non-commercial models in code (doc 35 §1)
Accountability Hash-chained audit log (HMAC keyed), immutable as-run, AI runs and decisions recorded, statutory retention triggers
Quality Large automated test suites; 548-capture design audit with 0 axe findings; role journeys 14/14

2.2 What is weak or risky

# Issue Why it matters for the next phase
W1 Never run in production, on a studio PC, on a phone or in GitHub CI. Every new capability multiplies untested paths. Production feedback must come first.
W2 Two divergent codebases (A kept, B in a bundle; doc HANDOVER §2). Porting from B is still open (T15–T22). New work should not start until the port list is closed or explicitly dropped.
W3 Provider handling is inconsistent. ADR-009 says contracts live in App\Infrastructure\*\Contracts; that folder does not exist. Contracts sit in five different shapes (Drivers, Providers, Contracts, Processing, Services). Contribution providers are a hard-coded enum (ContributionProvider: VDO.Ninja, StreamYard, phone, upload, other) with VDO.Ninja link logic inside ContributionService. This is the exact single-solution dependency your thesis warns about. It is the first refactor of the next phase (§5).
W4 "Off until keys" is not the same as "works". Dozens of integrations are built against documentation and faked HTTP, never against the real service. A capability should count as available only after a live health check passes (§5.3).
W5 Single server, single region. The scale-up path exists on paper (doc 28 §1.7) but has not been exercised. Tiers 2–4 need it rehearsed, including restore drills.
W6 The breadth is itself a risk. The platform has more features than most newsrooms ten times MediaOS's size. Each external integration needs someone to watch API changes, app reviews and token expiry. The tier model must keep the default set small. More options must not mean more things switched on.
W7 The DAM is a flat library. media_assets has strong rights fields but no folders, collections, retention classes or storage tiers, and the audit trail is not browsable per asset. Your archive requirement (§C) needs a real data model, not more filters.
W8 Comment moderation is rule-based only (CommentService::screen: blocked terms, links, shouting, repetition, duplicates). Fine for launch; not enough for millions of comments in 16 languages.
W9 No external contributor workflow. ContentType::Opinion exists, but every author must be a staff user. Your op-ed requirement needs a contributor identity and an intake desk (§B).
W10 Shared hosting is narrower than it sounds. MediaOS needs PostgreSQL 14+ with pg_trgm/unaccent and a Node runtime (doc 14 §1). Most cPanel hosting is MySQL-only. Tier 0 is "shared hosting that offers PostgreSQL and Node, or the cheapest VPS". Porting MediaOS to MySQL is not recommended: it would break search, JSONB blocks, triggers and the audit chain.

6.3The thesis, judged honestly

Your statement: a media platform should never depend on one external solution for any integrated capability; VDO.Ninja should be one option among many, in parallel.

Verdict: correct for capabilities that cross MediaOS's boundary to a third party, and costly if applied to MediaOS's own core. The rule that should govern the next phase:

Abstract at the boundary, standardise the core. Anything MediaOS does not control (an outside app, a platform, a vendor, a network) goes behind a MediaOS interface with at least two working providers and a manual fallback. Anything MediaOS runs itself as the system of record stays one well-chosen technology, upgraded in place.

3.1 Where pluggable providers pay off (do it)

Capability Why one provider is dangerous Evidence
Guest contribution (video and audio) Apps get blocked (Ethiopia has repeatedly blocked social and messaging platforms), change terms, or fail behind carrier NAT doc 33 §1, doc 28 §7 (TURN warning for VDO.Ninja on Ethiopian networks)
Live distribution and multistreaming Platform accounts get suspended or region-limited; Restream and StreamYard change plans doc 27 §4–5
Telephony and SMS Aggregators and short codes differ per country and carrier doc 40, PhoneGateway
Payments Already done: six rails doc 34
Object storage, CDN, e-mail Price and policy shocks; Cloudflare's terms restrict video on its CDN doc 28 §1.3
AI engines Models improve monthly; licences differ; Perspective API is being shut down §E
Human verification (captcha) Vendor outages or blocks would lock readers out of forms §D

3.2 Where it does not pay off (do not do it)

Component Why not What to do instead
Database (PostgreSQL) Search, JSONB, triggers, audit chain, pgvector all depend on it; an "any database" layer would remove the features that make MediaOS good Stay on PostgreSQL; scale it (replicas, PITR, managed service)
Application framework (Laravel, Next.js, Flutter) Rewrites, not swaps Upgrade in place on a schedule (§D)
Identity and permissions One model is a security property Add sign-in methods (passkeys, SSO), not identity providers
Design system and typography One voice is a brand property One system, themable per edition (§F)
Vision mixer internals OBS, Meld, vMix and hardware mixers differ deeply Keep the engine-neutral command set; add engines only when a studio actually runs one
Low-value integrations A driver for a platform nobody uses costs maintenance forever Add a provider only when a real outlet needs it, and remove dead ones

3.3 Costs that come with every extra provider

Each provider adds a credential to protect, a data flow to declare under PDPP 1321/2024, an API that will change, a test fake, a health check and a support burden. Providers also tempt a lowest-common-denominator interface that hides each tool's best feature. The design in §5 answers this with three rules:

  1. Small interfaces with optional capabilities, not one giant interface (a provider declares what it supports, for example "can produce a clean ISO feed", "can dial out", "has a director view").
  2. A manual provider for every capability. If every automated path fails, a person can still do the job with a checklist, and MediaOS still records it (the existing ManualGateway and ManualProvider are the model).
  3. Tier defaults keep the switched-on set small. An outlet sees all options, but runs two or three.

3.4 What your list did not mention and should be on the table

  • Return feeds and talkback (IFB, mix-minus). A guest on any app must hear the programme without their own voice echoed back. This is the hardest practical problem in remote interviews and decides which tools are usable (§A.3).
  • Live safety: delay and dump. Ethiopian law (2025 amendment) makes the outlet responsible during live transmission. MediaOS has a programme delay and DUMP command (LiveSafeguardService); every new guest route must pass through it.
  • Loudness and audio standards (EBU R128 / ITU-R BS.1770, −23 LUFS for broadcast, about −16 LUFS for streams and podcasts) so that a WhatsApp caller and a studio microphone sound like one programme.
  • Time and sync (NTP/PTP), so as-run, captions and multi-camera recordings line up.
  • Accessibility of live output: live captions and sign-language picture-in-picture (doc 33 #26).
  • Provenance: C2PA already exists; extend it to clips and archive exports.
  • Ad insertion markers (SCTE-35) for broadcast and FAST channels at Tier 3+.
  • Rights for guest material: the consent ledger in contribution_sessions must follow the recording into the archive and every clip (§C).
  • Exit and data portability: every provider must let MediaOS export its data, and MediaOS must export everything it holds (IPTC NewsML-G2/ninjs, EBUCore for media), so no vendor or host can trap the outlet.
  • Observability per capability: a capability is only "on" if it is monitored.

6.4Capability tier model

4.1 The five tiers

Tier Name Typical operator Infrastructure Monthly cost (order of magnitude, [verify])
0 Starter A small outlet, one to five people Shared hosting with PostgreSQL and Node (cPanel profile, doc 14) or the cheapest VPS; Cloudflare Free US$5–20
1 Newsroom MediaOS at launch One 8 vCPU / 16 GB VPS with the Docker kit (doc 28): MediaMTX, Icecast, ClamAV, optional self-hosted VDO.Ninja, Syncthing relay, CPU AI worker US$20–60
2 Network Several editions on air, daily live shows Separate media server; self-hosted Jitsi or LiveKit with a SIP gateway; object storage; managed or replicated PostgreSQL with point-in-time recovery; GPU on demand for AI; second web node US$150–600
3 Broadcaster 24/7 TV and radio channels, several studios Studio LAN with NDI or SMPTE ST 2110 video and AES67/Dante audio; playout servers; SRT gateways; bonded-cellular receivers; own SFTP and accelerated transfer; dedicated GPU; satellite uplink through a teleport partner US$2,000+ plus hardware
4 Global Many regions, very large audiences Multi-region active/standby, multi-CDN, regional media hubs, read replicas, 24/7 operations Contracted

The tiers are not editions of the software. Every tier runs the same code. A tier is a set of defaults: which providers are on, which compose profiles run, and which switches the Capabilities page offers. An outlet can mix tiers (for example Tier 1 hosting with a Tier 3 studio).

4.3 How a switch works ("click the button")

  1. Detect. Each provider declares its requirements (a compose profile running, a host reachable, a key present, a licence accepted, a minimum tier). A scheduled jmn:capabilities:probe command checks them and records health.
  2. Offer. Administration → Capabilities lists every capability. A provider whose requirements fail shows a checklist ("needs: media server reachable at stream.; SIP trunk credentials") with a link to the setup guide.
  3. Enable. When requirements pass, the switch becomes active. Turning it on needs capabilities.manage plus MFA, is audited, and can be scoped per edition through the existing Pennant flags.
  4. Fall back. Each capability has an ordered provider chain. If the active provider's health check fails, MediaOS offers (never silently performs, for live production) the next provider, and always the manual one.
  5. Disable safely. Turning a provider off never deletes its data; sessions, recordings and logs stay readable.

What the button cannot do: buy a server, sign a vendor contract, obtain a Meta business verification or a broadcast licence. Those stay owner actions, and the checklist says so.

6.5The provider abstraction layer

5.1 One registry for all capabilities

Today each domain has its own registry. The next phase adds one shared mechanism in app/Support/Capabilities (the "Capability Registry") and moves every existing registry onto it without changing behaviour:

Existing Becomes
Social\Drivers\SocialDriverRegistry Capability social.publish and video.upload
Revenue\Providers\GatewayRegistry Capability payments
Live\Providers\LiveProviderRegistry Capability live.hosting
Tts\Contracts\TtsEngine drivers Capability ai.tts
Phone\Contracts\PhoneGateway Capability telephony.sms, telephony.voice
Search\Services\SearchEngine Capability search
Media\Processing\MediaProcessor Capability media.transcode
Security\Scanning\MalwareScanner Capability security.malware_scan
Provenance\Contracts\ContentCredentialsTool Capability provenance.sign
Broadcast\Enums\ContributionProvider (enum, VDO.Ninja logic in ContributionService) New capability live.contribution with real drivers
Broadcast\Enums\StudioEngine Capability studio.engine
Broadcast\Enums\StreamPlatform Capability live.distribution

New capabilities: live.media_hub, live.multistream, live.interaction, dam.storage_tier, transfer, ai.ocr, ai.moderation, ai.image, ai.translation, ai.stt (moved from the worker client), security.human_check, edge.cdn_purge, edge.image_transform, notify.channel.

5.2 Common provider contract

Every provider implements a small base contract; each capability adds its own contract on top (full PHP in G see Product Bible):

  • key(), capability(), label(), licence() (open source, freemium, commercial), minimumTier()
  • requirements(): list<Requirement> (compose profile, host, credential, accepted terms, tier)
  • health(): HealthReport (ok, degraded, down, with a message an operator understands)
  • features(): list<string> (optional abilities such as iso_feed, dial_out, director, recording)
  • dataFlows(): list<DataFlow> (what personal data leaves MediaOS, to which country; feeds the PDPP processing register, Compliance\Services\ProcessingRegister)

5.3 Rules every provider must follow

  1. Credentials live only in the encrypted settings store (doc 42 E15), never in code, logs or files. No API key is ever written to a document or repository.

  2. Each provider has a contract test against a fake and a live probe that can run in staging.

  3. A provider is "available" only after its live probe has passed in the last 24 hours.

  4. Every external call goes through the existing outbound URL guard (SSRF protection) and has a timeout.

  5. Each provider declares its data flows; enabling one that sends personal data abroad shows the PDPP warning.

  6. Every capability has a manual provider.

  7. Providers are removed when unused for two releases, after export.

6.7Phased roadmap

Sizes as in doc 33: S ≤ 1 developer-week, M 2–5, L 6+. Phases overlap only where dependencies allow.

Status (6 November 2026): release 1.3.0 built phase 1, phase 2 (2.4 in part) and items 3.5 and 3.6; the item-by-item status is in REMAINING-TASKS.md.

Phase 0 — Finish and deploy 1.2.0 (in progress; not part of this plan's budget)

Backlog tasks T1–T4 (baseline on the PC, commit, repository and CI, security cross-check), T15–T22 port decisions, first production deployment, studio rehearsal (T29), phone tests (T30), media servers (T31). Exit gate: MediaOS runs in production for at least four weeks with backups restored once.

Phase 1 — Foundations for switchable capabilities (about 10–12 developer-weeks)

Phase 4 — AI layer (about 10–14 developer-weeks, mostly in the AI worker)

OCR (PaddleOCR or Surya, evaluated on Amharic and Arabic newsprint), subtitle translation from the existing STT + MADLAD pipeline, image enhancement and smart crop, moderation model service, fraud and intrusion signals with CrowdSec and application-level scoring. Detail in E.

Phase 5 — Broadcaster (about 20+ developer-weeks plus hardware)

Hardware control through Studio Bridge and Bitfocus Companion (PTZ cameras via VISCA over IP, recorders such as HyperDeck, audio consoles via OSC); NDI and AES67 on the studio LAN; 24/7 playout (Liquidsoap for radio, CasparCG for TV, already integrated); SCTE-35 markers; bonded-cellular receivers (SRTLA); accelerated file transfer; satellite distribution through a teleport over SRT; a broadcast phone system for talk shows. Detail in A §7–9.

Phase 6 — Global

Multi-region active/standby with PostgreSQL replicas, regional media hubs, multi-CDN with health-based steering, regional AI pools, 24/7 operations runbooks. Plan this only when traffic data justifies it.

6.9How to use this document

  • It governs the next phase. A change to the plan is made here first, then built.
  • Each phase item becomes tasks in REMAINING-TASKS.md when its phase starts, one commit per task with tests, as now.
  • Every item that creates an outside account, spends money, publishes, or touches production waits for the owner.
  • Review the plan at the end of each phase against production data.

Provider interfaces

7.1  Capability Registry (app/Support/Capabilities)7.2  Live contribution (App\Domain\Broadcast\Contribution)7.3  Media hub and distribution7.4  Interaction sources7.5  AI capabilities7.6  Other boundaries

Part of doc 44 see Product Bible. These are the contracts to build in Phase 1. They follow the existing conventions (doc 18): strict types, App\Domain\* modules, ApiException envelopes, AuditLogger, PermissionService, tests in tests/Feature. Names are proposals; keep them stable once merged.

7.1Capability Registry (app/Support/Capabilities)

namespace App\Support\Capabilities;

enum Tier: int { case Starter = 0; case Newsroom = 1; case Network = 2; case Broadcaster = 3; case Global = 4; }

enum Licence: string { case OpenSource = 'open_source'; case Freemium = 'freemium'; case Commercial = 'commercial'; case Manual = 'manual'; }

/** A thing that must be true before a provider can be enabled. */
final readonly class Requirement
{
    public function __construct(
        public string $kind,      // compose_profile | host | credential | terms | tier | extension | owner_action
        public string $key,       // e.g. 'livekit', 'stream.horndaily.example:8890', 'LIVEKIT_API_SECRET'
        public string $label,     // operator-readable, translated in the UI
        public ?string $docUrl = null,
    ) {}
}

final readonly class HealthReport
{
    /** @param 'ok'|'degraded'|'down'|'unconfigured' $state */
    public function __construct(public string $state, public string $message, public array $details = [], public ?\DateTimeImmutable $checkedAt = null) {}
}

/** What personal data leaves JMN through this provider (feeds Compliance\Services\ProcessingRegister). */
final readonly class DataFlow
{
    public function __construct(public string $category, public string $recipient, public string $country, public string $purpose) {}
}

interface Provider
{
    public function key(): string;                 // 'vdo_ninja', 'livekit', 'asterisk', …
    public function capability(): string;          // 'live.contribution'
    public function label(): string;
    public function licence(): Licence;
    public function minimumTier(): Tier;
    /** @return list<Requirement> */
    public function requirements(): array;
    /** @return list<string> optional abilities, e.g. iso_feed, dial_out, director, recording, sip */
    public function features(): array;
    /** @return list<DataFlow> */
    public function dataFlows(): array;
    /** Live probe; must be cheap, time-limited and never change state. */
    public function health(): HealthReport;
}

final class CapabilityRegistry
{
    /** @param iterable<Provider> $providers tagged in a service provider */
    public function __construct(private iterable $providers, private CapabilitySettings $settings) {}

    /** Providers for a capability, in the configured fallback order. @return list<Provider> */
    public function chain(string $capability, ?string $languageId = null): array { /* … */ }

    /** The active provider, or the manual one when nothing else is enabled and healthy. */
    public function active(string $capability, ?string $languageId = null): Provider { /* … */ }

    public function enable(string $capability, string $providerKey, \App\Domain\Identity\Models\User $by, ?string $languageId = null): void { /* checks requirements + recent healthy probe, MFA ability, audits */ }
}

Storage: capability_settings (capability, provider_key, language_id nullable, enabled, position, options jsonb, enabled_by, enabled_at, lock_version) and capability_probes (provider_key, state, message, details, checked_at; pruned after 30 days). Credentials stay in the encrypted settings store.

Commands: jmn:capabilities:probe (scheduled every 5 minutes for enabled providers, hourly for the rest), jmn:capabilities:list. Permission: capabilities.manage (sensitive, MFA). Admin page: Administration → Capabilities (grouped by area, tier badges, requirement checklists, health history, enable/disable per edition).

7.2Live contribution (App\Domain\Broadcast\Contribution)

Replaces the ContributionProvider enum and moves VDO.Ninja link building out of ContributionService.

interface ContributionDriver extends Provider
{
    /** Create provider-side resources (room, token, SIP route) for a session. Idempotent per session id. */
    public function open(ContributionSession $s): OpenedSession;
    /** What the guest receives: a link, a phone number + PIN, or recipe steps for the producer. */
    public function guestInvite(ContributionSession $s, string $locale): GuestInvite;
    /** Director / producer view, if any. */
    public function controlView(ContributionSession $s): ?string;
    /** How the studio or media hub receives this guest: SRT/WHEP/RTMP URL, NDI name, browser-source URL, or 'manual'. */
    public function programFeed(ContributionSession $s): FeedEndpoint;
    /** Optional: dial the guest (phone, WhatsApp). Throws when features() lacks 'dial_out'. */
    public function dialOut(ContributionSession $s): void;
    public function close(ContributionSession $s): void;
    /** Normalise provider callbacks (joined, left, recording ready) into ContributionEvent, or null if unsigned. */
    public function parseWebhook(\Illuminate\Http\Request $r): ?ContributionEvent;
}

Drivers: VdoNinjaDriver, JitsiDriver (public and self-hosted with JWT), LiveKitDriver, GaleneDriver, SipBridgeDriver (Asterisk/FreeSWITCH via ARI or ESL), WhatsAppCallingDriver, SrtFieldDriver, StreamYardLinkDriver, RecipeDriver (Zoom, Teams, Meet, WhatsApp desktop, Telegram, phone hybrid: returns steps), UploadDriver. contribution_sessions.provider becomes a string key validated against the registry; existing rows keep their values (vdo_ninja, streamyard, phone, upload, other), so the migration is additive.

7.3Media hub and distribution

interface MediaHub extends Provider
{
    public function ensurePath(string $name, PathPolicy $policy): void;          // credentials, recording, max readers
    public function publishUrl(string $name, string $protocol): string;          // srt | whip | rtmp | rist
    public function playbackUrl(string $name, string $protocol): string;         // hls | whep | srt
    public function stats(string $name): PathStats;                              // bitrate, loss, readers, last frame
    public function removePath(string $name): void;

interface MultistreamProvider extends Provider
{
    /** @param list<StreamDestination> $targets */
    public function start(string $sourcePath, array $targets): MultistreamRun;
    public function stop(MultistreamRun $run, ?StreamDestination $only = null): void;
    public function status(MultistreamRun $run): array;   // per-destination state for the as-run log
}

Drivers: MediaMtxHub (wraps the existing MediaMtxApi), later SrsHub / OvenMediaHub; SelfFanOutProvider (MediaMTX hooks + FFmpeg), RestreamProvider (wraps RestreamService), MeldMultiProvider (manual), LiveKitEgressProvider.

7.4Interaction sources

interface InteractionSource extends Provider
{
    /** Start following a context (live video id, chat id). */
    public function follow(InteractionContext $ctx): void;
    public function unfollow(InteractionContext $ctx): void;
    /** Pull-based sources: fetch new events since the cursor. @return array{events: list<InteractionEvent>, cursor: ?string} */
    public function poll(InteractionContext $ctx, ?string $cursor): array;
    /** Push-based sources: verify and normalise a webhook. @return list<InteractionEvent> */
    public function parseWebhook(\Illuminate\Http\Request $r): array;
    /** Optional moderation back on the platform (features: delete, ban, reply). */
    public function act(InteractionEvent $e, string $action, ?string $reply = null): void;
}

Drivers: SiteCommentsSource, YouTubeLiveChatSource, FacebookLiveSource, TwitchSource, TelegramSource, WhatsAppBusinessSource, RestreamChatSource, SmsSource, GenericWebhookSource (for Social Stream Ninja and similar).

7.5AI capabilities

The worker keeps its HTTP API; the API side gets one small interface per task so cloud and self-hosted engines are interchangeable:

interface OcrEngine extends Provider { public function recognise(string $path, ?string $language): OcrResult; }
interface ModerationClassifier extends Provider { public function classify(string $text, string $language, string $context): ModerationScores; }
interface TranslationEngine extends Provider { public function translate(TranslationRequest $r): TranslationResult; }

// TtsEngine exists (App\Domain\Tts\Contracts) and gains the Provider base.

Every call still goes through AiWorkerGovernance / AiAssistant (permissions, flags, budgets, confidentiality, immutable ai_runs).

8.1Local setup (Linux)

# Services
sudo service postgresql start && sudo service redis-server start
# One-time DB
sudo -u postgres psql -c "CREATE ROLE jmn LOGIN PASSWORD 'jmn_dev_password' CREATEDB;"
sudo -u postgres createdb -O jmn jmn && sudo -u postgres createdb -O jmn jmn_test
for d in jmn jmn_test; do sudo -u postgres psql -d $d -c "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm; CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent; CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS citext;"; done
# API
cd apps/api && cp .env.example .env && composer install && php artisan key:generate
php artisan migrate --seed
pm2 start ../../ecosystem.config.cjs     # api on :8000, web on :3000
# Web
cd apps/web && cp .env.example .env.local && npm ci && npm run build
The development seeder creates demo staff (see DemoSeeder) with the password taken from JMN_DEMO_PASSWORD.

Browser tests (Playwright + axe)

cd apps/web && npx playwright install --with-deps chromium   # once
# API (:8000), web (:3000, built) and the scheduler running, demo data seeded (APP_ENV=local)
npm run test:e2e                     # all specs, desktop + mobile
npm run test:a11y                    # axe only
JMN_E2E_BASE_URL=https://staging.example.org npm run test:e2e   # against another stack (demo accounts required)
Set JMN_RENDER_KEY to the same value in apps/api/.env and apps/web/.env.local. Otherwise the suite's page loads share one per-IP API limit and hit 429.

8.2Standards

  • PHP: declare(strict_types=1), final classes by default, typed properties and returns, no business logic in controllers, and no DB::raw with user input.
  • Always use FormRequests and $this->authorize() or Policies. Never rely on route visibility.
  • Money is stored in integer micros. Times are UTC.
  • TypeScript: strict, no any in src/lib, and server-only modules import 'server-only'.
  • Commits follow Conventional Commits (feat(editorial): ...) and reference REQ IDs.

8.3Definition of Done (spec §203)

A task is Done only when all of these hold:

  1. Its migrations and constraints exist.

  2. Its service, API and policy are implemented.

  3. Its UI is implemented, where applicable.

  4. It is localised (no hard-coded UI strings in components; they go through the dictionary).

  5. It is accessible (keyboard, labels, contrast).

  6. It has tests for the happy path, the authorization failure and the edge cases.

  7. Pint, Larastan and the tests are green, and tsc, ESLint and the build are green.

  8. The docs are updated (the spec doc plus the doc 17 tracker).

  9. It is audited where it is security-relevant.

9.1  Conventions9.2  Envelope9.3  Endpoint catalogue (v1)9.4  Webhooks (§75) (implemented, phase 22)9.5  Rate limits (§127)9.6  OpenAPI (implemented, phase 22)9.7  Newsletters9.8  Audience (readers)9.9  Audio/video and podcasts9.10  Live events9.11  Advertising9.12  Analytics9.13  Email Center (October 2026)

9.1Conventions

  • Base path /api/v1. JSON only. UTF-8. Times in ISO-8601 UTC.
  • Every response carries an X-Request-Id header, echoed from the client when it matches ^[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,64}$, otherwise generated as a ULID.
  • Auth: Authorization: Bearer <token> (Sanctum). Staff tokens carry abilities; admin endpoints require MFA-verified tokens (mfa ability) when MFA is enforced for the role.
  • Locale: ?lang=am or the Accept-Language header.
  • Pagination: ?page[size]=20&page[cursor]=... (cursor) for feeds; ?page=2&per_page=20 for admin lists. The meta field carries {per_page, next_cursor|current_page,total}.
  • Filtering: ?filter[status]=published&filter[language]=am. Sorting: ?sort=-published_at.
  • Concurrency: send lock_version in the mutation body. A mismatch returns 409 EDIT_CONFLICT with details.current.
  • Idempotency: Idempotency-Key header (≤128 visible ASCII characters) on create-style POST/PATCH routes — newsroom article create, upload sessions, assignments (create, edit, status, file), desk chat posts, studio as-run and uploads, push device registration (middleware idempotent, table idempotent_requests). The key is scoped to the caller (staff user, studio device, or client address); an identical retry within 24 h gets the stored status and body with Idempotent-Replayed: true; the same key with a different body is 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED; a duplicate while the first is still running is 409 IDEMPOTENCY_IN_PROGRESS (Retry-After: 1); 5xx responses are not stored. Expired keys are pruned hourly (jmn:idempotency:prune).

9.2Envelope

Success 

{ "success": true, "data": {...}, "meta": {...}, "request_id": "01J..." }
Error (spec §125) 
{ "success": false, "error": { "code": "ARTICLE_NOT_FOUND", "message": "...", "details": {} }, "request_id": "01J..." }
Standard codes: VALIDATION_FAILED(422), UNAUTHENTICATED(401), MFA_REQUIRED(401), FORBIDDEN(403), NOT_FOUND/<ENTITY>_NOT_FOUND(404), EDIT_CONFLICT(409), INVALID_TRANSITION(409), EMBARGO_ACTIVE(409), RATE_LIMITED(429), ACCOUNT_LOCKED(423), SERVER_ERROR(500), NOT_INSTALLED(503). 500-level responses never include stack traces or internal messages.

POST /newsroom/investigations/{id}/notes append-only; supersedes_id for corrections
POST/DELETE /newsroom/investigations/{id}/articles[/{articleId}] link stories (publication gate)
GET/POST/PATCH /newsroom/investigations/{id}/sources[/{sourceId}] alias-level; create or link source_id
POST /newsroom/investigations/{id}/sources/{sourceId}/reveal MFA, reason, 5/min
POST /newsroom/investigations/{id}/sources/{sourceId}/purge MFA, reason, confirm_alias; irreversible
GET /newsroom/investigations/{id}/sources/{sourceId}/access-log owner / lead

Errors: LEGAL_CLEARANCE_REQUIRED, CLEARANCE_LOCKED, SOURCE_PURGED, CODENAME_TAKEN, ALIAS_TAKEN, LEAD_REQUIRED, ALREADY_MEMBER.

9.4Webhooks (§75) (implemented, phase 22)

Events: - article.published, article.updated, article.corrected, article.unpublished and breaking.published (one per edition); - video.ready, podcast.published, newsletter.sent, live.started and live.ended; - ping (test only).

Request: - Method and headers: POST JSON with X-JMN-Event, X-JMN-Delivery (one per delivery), X-JMN-Event-Id (stable across endpoints, retries and redeliveries) and X-JMN-Timestamp. - Signature: X-JMN-Signature: sha256=hex(HMAC_SHA256(secret, timestamp + "." + raw_body)). Receivers compare in constant time and reject timestamps more than 5 minutes off. - Body: {id, type, created_at, api_version, data}, carrying public data only.

Delivery: - Durable rows in webhook_deliveries; the queue carries only ids, and claims are atomic, so a delivery is never sent twice in parallel. - Success is any 2xx within 10 s. Redirects are not followed. - Retries after 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h and 12 h; the delivery is abandoned after the 6th attempt. Every attempt is logged in webhook_attempts. - jmn:webhooks:dispatch-due runs every minute: it re-dispatches due rows, releases stale claims and prunes history older than 30 days. - Circuit breaker: 10 consecutive failures disable the endpoint and abandon its queue. Re-enabling resets it.

SSRF protection: - URLs must be public https, use port 443 or a port ≥ 1024, and carry no credentials. - Loopback, private, link-local, CGNAT, multicast, reserved and IPv6 ULA/link-local/mapped addresses are refused. - DNS is resolved and checked on create and again on every attempt, and the connection is pinned to the vetted IP (CURLOPT_RESOLVE) to defeat DNS rebinding.

Admin API (settings.manage + MFA): - GET|POST /admin/webhooks. - GET|PATCH|DELETE /admin/webhooks/{id} (PATCH needs lock_version; is_active: true re-enables). - POST /admin/webhooks/{id}/rotate-secret. - POST /admin/webhooks/{id}/ping. - GET /admin/webhooks/deliveries/{id} (payload + attempt history). - POST /admin/webhooks/deliveries/{id}/redeliver. - Secrets are stored encrypted and returned only on create and rotation. Every change is audited. - Error codes: 422 URL_INVALID, URL_HOST, URL_PRIVATE, URL_PORT, URL_UNRESOLVABLE, EVENTS_INVALID, LANGUAGE_UNKNOWN; 409 EDIT_CONFLICT.

9.6OpenAPI (implemented, phase 22)

  • dedoc/scramble generates OpenAPI 3.1 from routes, validation rules and responses: php artisan scramble:export writes apps/api/resources/openapi/jmn-v1.json, which is committed.
  • GET /api/v1/openapi.json serves it, adding an x-webhooks section (event catalogue, headers, retry policy).
  • The contract test WebhookTest::test_openapi_document_covers_every_v1_route fails when any /api/v1 route is missing, so every new endpoint must be re-exported.
  • Developer portal on the web: /developers (overview, quick start, conventions, errors), /developers/reference (filterable list of all operations by area and access) and /developers/reference/{area} (parameters, JSON body fields, constraints, curl example, responses). /developers/webhooks covers the event catalogue, a sample request, verification code in Node, PHP and Python, and the delivery and retry semantics. /developers/openapi.json is the same-origin download.
  • The portal is server-rendered with no client JavaScript, and NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL sets the base URL shown in examples.
